prompt_text: How to set up tribute and memorial giving
response_text:
Here’s a clear, practical overview of how to set up tribute and memorial giving, whether you’re:

- an individual/family creating a memorial fund for one person, or  
- a nonprofit creating an ongoing tribute/memorial giving program.

---

## Part 1: For Individuals/Families – Memorial Fund for a Loved One

### 1. Decide the Purpose and Beneficiary

Clarify what the memorial giving is for:

- Support funeral/medical expenses  
- Donate to a specific charity/NGO  
- Create something tangible (bench, tree, scholarship, brick, etc.)  
- Launch a small ongoing fund (e.g., annual scholarship in their name)

This will shape where and how you set things up.

### 2. Choose a Platform or Structure

Common options:

1. **Crowdfunding platforms** (e.g., GoFundMe, Givebutter)
   - Fastest to set up
   - Good for funeral costs or one-time memorial projects
   - Read fee structures and payout timelines

2. **Direct donations to an existing charity**
   - Ask the charity if they can accept “in memory of” gifts and track them under your loved one’s name  
   - Many nonprofits already have “tribute” or “in memory” options on their forms

3. **Formal memorial fund / scholarship**
   - With a community foundation, school, or nonprofit  
   - More work, often needs a minimum amount to start  
   - Better if you want something long-term and structured

### 3. Set Up the Memorial Page / Fund

If using an online fundraiser:

- **Title**: “[Name] Memorial Fund” or “In Memory of [Name] – [Purpose]”
- **Story**:
  - Who they were (briefly)  
  - Why you’re raising funds and what they will support  
  - Your relationship to them  
  - How funds will be used and distributed (be specific and transparent)
- **Photos/Videos**: Choose a few that reflect their personality and life, not only their obituary photo.
- **Goal amount**: 
  - Estimate funeral or project costs, or  
  - Set a symbolic goal (e.g., $5,000 for a scholarship seed fund)

If directing donations to a charity:

- Ask the charity:
  - How people should designate gifts (e.g., “In memory of [Name]”)  
  - Whether you can have a dedicated page or link  
  - Whether they will notify you/your family when donations come in

### 4. Decide How You’ll Acknowledge Gifts

Even small touches matter:

- Thank donors personally (short email or note)
- If appropriate, send a brief note to close family summarizing gifts received in their loved one’s name
- Consider a simple update to donors after:
  - The funeral/celebration of life, or  
  - The project is completed (bench installed, tree planted, scholarship awarded)

### 5. Share the Memorial Giving Option

Use clear, simple wording and repeat it wherever people look for information:

- **Obituary and service announcement**  
  Example:  
  “In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial donations to [Fund/Charity Name]. Gifts may be made at [URL] or by check to [instructions].”

- **Funeral program / order of service**  
- **Social media & email**:  
  Share the link with a short message about what the memorial donations will support.

### 6. Create a Lasting Tribute (Optional but Powerful)

Consider how the money will create something visible or ongoing:

- A park bench, memorial brick, or tree in a meaningful place  
- An annual donation to a cause they loved  
- An award or scholarship in their name (even informal, e.g., a yearly prize at a local school)

Document it: photos, a short write-up, and share with donors so they see the impact of their gifts.

---

## Part 2: For Nonprofits – Tribute & Memorial Giving Program

If you’re a nonprofit, you want **tribute/“in honor of”** and **memorial/“in memory of”** giving to be:

- Easy for donors  
- Recognized respectfully  
- Integrated into your regular fundraising

### 1. Make Tribute & Memorial Giving Visible Everywhere

Add options like:

> “My gift is: □ In honor of   □ In memory of  
> Honoree’s name: __________  
> Please notify: Name/Address/Email”

Place this on:

- Online donation forms  
- Reply devices in mailings  
- Newsletter reply envelopes (under the flap)  
- Event registration forms

Mention in communications:  
“Gifts in honor or memory of loved ones are always welcome.”

### 2. Build a Simple Internal Process

Your database or CRM should:

- Flag tribute/memorial gifts
- Store:
  - Donor
  - Honoree (person being honored/remembered)
  - Notification recipient (family or honoree)
- Trigger:
  - Thank-you to donor  
  - Notification to the family/honoree  

If you use fundraising software, check for a **“Tributes”** or **“In Honor Of”** module.

### 3. Create Two Standard Letters/Emails

1. **Donor Acknowledgment Letter**  
   - Thanks the donor  
   - Confirms that the gift is in honor/memory of [Name]  
   - Includes tax language as needed  

2. **Notification Letter to the Honoree/Family**  
   - Sensitive and brief  
   - Names the donor (unless you promise anonymity)  
   - Does *not* include the gift amount unless expressly requested  
   - Explains your mission in one or two sentences, and what their loved one’s tribute supports

Tone: gentle, timely, simple. Avoid overly fundraising-heavy language in these letters.

### 4. Recognize Tribute & Memorial Gifts Publicly (With Care)

Common methods:

- A “Tributes” section in your newsletter or annual report:
  - “In memory of [Name] – gifts received from [list optional]”
- Website recognition page
- Physical displays for cumulative giving levels (e.g., memorial wall, plaque, tree, or donor board)

Always:

- Get clear consent or follow your privacy policy
- Offer opt-out for public recognition

### 5. Train Staff and Volunteers

Make sure everyone knows:

- How to process a tribute/memorial gift  
- How to talk about the option when asked (funerals, weddings, birthdays, holidays)  
- The emotional context—this is sensitive and often time-limited (around a loss or life event)

### 6. Promote Tribute Giving for Specific Occasions

Common occasions:

- In memory of someone who has died  
- Birthdays  
- Anniversaries (wedding, sobriety, recovery, other milestones)  
- Religious holidays (Christmas, Hanukkah, Eid, etc.)  
- “In lieu of gifts” for weddings, retirements, graduations

You can:

- Create seasonal campaigns: “Give a gift in honor of someone you love”  
- Add tribute language to holiday appeals and event materials  
- Offer e-cards or printed cards that donors can send to honorees

### 7. Track, Steward, and Grow

Monitor:

- How many tribute/memorial gifts you receive  
- How donors found out about the option (envelopes, website, obituaries, etc.)  
- Which recognition methods prompt more giving (newsletter lists, memorial wall, etc.)

Then:

- Refine your forms and letters  
- Consider specialized landing pages: “Give in memory of someone special”  
- Build relationships with:
  - Funeral homes  
  - Clergy/faith communities  
  - Event planners  

So they know your organization is tribute-gift–friendly and has a clear process.

---

## Quick Templates

**Obituary / Service Line:**

> In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial donations to [Organization/Fund Name], supporting [purpose]. Contributions may be made online at [URL] or by check payable to “[Organization]” with “In memory of [Name]” in the memo.

**Nonprofit Website Line:**

> You can honor or remember someone special with a tribute gift. Simply select “In honor of” or “In memory of” on our donation form and provide the name and contact information of the person you’d like us to notify.

---

If you tell me whether you’re an individual/family or a nonprofit (and your country/region), I can help you sketch a simple, customized setup and wording you can copy-paste into your website, obituary, or forms.
